chapter: Becoming a player; Rene, Bunk and Armstrong
title: 1921 visit to New Orleans, Rene's C-sharp blues and Armstrong's Chloe
summary: On his first return home he heard Rene, then talks about keys, Armstrong's Chloe solo and Mud Carrier.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Buddy Bolden and Buddy Petit: the trumpet legends

blocks.x: Well then, I'll tell you what happened. I've forgotten about this. I returned in the Orleans in 1921. That's when I met Chester's artists. They were advertising. And I rode on the truck. While I'm still in the preliminary stages. So. You hadn't played any jobs yet. Well I played some with a little band, with Bernie Young, Al Simeon, Omar Simeon, Jimmy McHenry, and people like that, you know. And we were non-union. Just 15? Yeah, we were non-union then. Well we could read a little. You see, yeah, we was reading a little bit. Because we had to be, when we all went in there, this business there, a big tall fella about down there eight feet named Monroe. He chased his catches on them jobs, you know, and run us off the job. So it finally ran us into the union. So we had to take examination. Oh yeah. And Clarence Jones, great pianist, had the band at the Howard's Theater. He was one of the guys that examined us. They put the music right up there and we had to play it. And we played it. So I came back to New Orleans and I was with Renny every day. Get Renny every day. He was playing up in San Susie. And we placed some girls right up there, me and Clarence, right in the neighborhood where I was raised. We'd go to their house every day and Renny and them liked wine and stuff. And I never cared much for the strong stuff, you know. I'm a sweet guy. I like a chemical or something sweet, you know. If it was wine, it was a sweet wine I'd like. But so I hung around Renny and I sent him with Maurice French. Now I love this play. It was a trombone play, wasn't it? No, a trombone play. It was a good one too. He played that, Renny played, My Muscle's Loom It On. And Maurice would sing against the middle of the sea. You know, a regular obligato right with it. Maurice is a nice trombone play. And they had Zepp Renneas I think is his name. And one of the Mareros, he's a Simon, he's a brother. And Joe Renne and Renne himself, no piano. So they played about two or three nights a week up there to San Susie. And I was around about a month or so, I had Bernie Young send some music. But some of the guys in the band didn't read, you know. But I used to like to hear them play Climax, Rag. And Renne and them used to play the blues in C sharp. Now that's the thing about a lot of them guitar players around here, them blues singers. They can't play with us and we can't play with them because they don't have no particular key. Wherever they pick out a melody, a lot of them D flat or G flat or C sharp or F sharp or E natural, anything you know. And let's face it, the average musician has his pet tunes and his pet keys. There's some keys that we all can play better than others. And a B flat instrument, sharp usually bother them if they're not playing them right regularly, you know. And so that's why I never could play with Muddy Waters or some of those blues artists around Chicago because you don't know what key you're playing. And unless you practice playing them keys, and you don't practice as much playing those keys as you would, and a more easier key such as B flat, E flat, F, C natural, even G. You understand what I'm talking about? But most of the stuff is there. Now Fletcher Henderson, a lot of guys complained about his music because he said that the sharp was beautiful, you know, it was more beautiful than the flats. So a lot of his stuff, I read some of his music, a lot of his stuff was in E and D and C sharp and like that, see what I'm talking about? But there's a general rule that I was going to play the blues, the guy coming right now and said I'm going to play, he'll play the blues even B flat or E flat. Either one of those keys. He won't take the C sharp. Well Rene, Rene was stout, he was a little small. See, he and Buddy Petit was around the same size. I heard Buddy, but I didn't know who he was. Now I actually said about, especially the fellas from downtown, say that Rene was better than Louis Armstrong. But I don't agree with him. First thing, Louis' range was greater. And I'd go to say that his tone was more beautiful. Louis Armstrong had a beautiful tone. And Louis Armstrong, we were at the Surviving Garden right there and we had Chloe. Chloe's in D flat. He comes right back to what I was saying. Now, it's tunes I can play very well, you know, our solos, our solos, in D flat. And it's some team tunes that are warming too. So it's Chloe, he passed out the music. He had a photograph in mind when I'm coming to it. And we played it, we played the music down, then he began to pass out the solos. Well we wasn't used to playing that. Well Stardust is D flat, you know, and we played Stardust and like that. But this Chloe, da da da da da da da da da da da da da da. He played in C down there. Yeah, well D flat. So well you know, he'd play a tune down once and turn the music over and play it right down like he was looking at the music. So all of us fell down by the wayside but him. That man played one of the prettiest solos on that Chloe that ever heard. And falling in love and things like that. Ding dong daddy. All them things back in there you know. He was really playing there you know. But later on he became a commercial you know. And that's where he made his money. See all that pretty stuff he was making and running things. The public is, don't understand jazz music as well as they should. They don't know where the fellas are making you know what I'm talking about. But they say that, see the boy that died in 31 was down here, buddy, I suppose over ate him, some people say ate himself to death. I wouldn't say that because I don't know that. It was alleged that he did that you know. So that makes it better for me. But he wasn't very strong. No, he was like Mud Carrier. Mud Carrier wasn't. Now Mud Carrier made Joe throw his horn away one day. Really? Yeah, Mud Carrier. Well Mud Carrier would take a glass, an ordinary glass like that and get a lot of sounds out of it just like Joe Oliver. But he was low like George Mitchell. You ever heard of George Mitchell when Joe was wrong? He wasn't very strong. You understand? And he'd get out on that low register there and run you crazy. So Joe said. You mean I would play Joe? Oh yeah, well Joe would stop me pawn chopping and get in my horn. And he said, well he can use your enjoyment. And he couldn't much worry to death. Now Willie Hightower was sweet jazz. You ever hear his play? Yeah, on record. Sweet, yeah. He used to be sweet. Played the blues. Yeah, sweet.
